- When sentiment is consistently bearish (negative or low) and model forecasts remain flat or upward, adjust downward by 2–5% to account for suppressed demand or policy-induced sell-off.  
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >5% from prior period), model tends to overcorrect — reduce forecast slope by 10–20% for next 5–7 days to avoid overshoot.  
- If official event net supply is negative and bearish sentiment dominates, model underestimates downside risk — add 3–8% downward bias to forecast mean.  
- When sentiment shifts from bullish to bearish mid-period, model often lags — apply a 1–3 day lag correction by lowering forecast 1–2% per day until sentiment stabilizes.  
- If model forecast is rising steadily but true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days of decline), reduce forecast slope by 15–25% for next 7 days.  
- For multi-day event windows (e.g., 3+ auction events), model tends to overestimate supply impact — reduce forecast by 5–10% for each additional event beyond 2.  
- If sentiment is neutral or mixed, model often overestimates volatility — cap forecast range within ±2% of recent 7-day average to avoid overreaction.
